item.question: Check if a triangle exists for each of the following set of lengths: (a) 1, 100, 100 (b) 3, 6, 9 (c) 1, 1, 5 (d) 5, 10, 12
steps_tex: $(a)$: The longest is $100$ and $1 + 100 = 101 > 100$: a triangle exists.
$(b)$: The longest is $9$ and $3 + 6 = 9$, equal to $9$: the circles touch, so no triangle.
$(c)$: The longest is $5$ and $1 + 1 = 2 < 5$: no triangle.
$(d)$: The longest is $12$ and $5 + 10 = 15 > 12$: a triangle exists.
item.answer_tex: Triangles exist for $(a)$ and $(d)$; not for $(b)$ (circles touch) or $(c)$

item.question: Does there exist an equilateral triangle with sides 50, 50, 50? In general, does there exist an equilateral triangle of any sidelength? Justify your answer.
steps_tex: For $50$, $50$, $50$ the longest is $50$ and the other two add to $50 + 50 = 100$.
$50 < 100$, so the triangle inequality holds and an equilateral triangle exists.
For any side length $s$ the other two add to $s + s = 2s$, and $s < 2s$ as long as $s$ is more than zero.
So the circles always cross: an equilateral triangle exists for every side length. It can be built with the two-arcs method of the first topic.
item.answer_tex: Yes: $50 < 50 + 50$, and in general $s < s + s$ for any side length $s$ above zero

item.question: A triangle has two sides of 6 cm and 5 cm that meet at a corner, and the angle at that corner is 30°. Is 30° the included angle? What if the 30° angle were at the other end of the 6 cm side?
steps: The two given sides, 6 cm and 5 cm, meet at one corner. The angle at that corner is between them, so 30° is the included angle.
If the 30° angle were at the other end of the 6 cm side, one of its arms would be the 6 cm side but the other arm would be a side that is not given.
That angle is not between the two given sides, so it is not the included angle. The measurements would then be a different kind of data.
item.answer: Yes, 30° is included when it sits between the 6 cm and 5 cm sides; at the other end it is not

steps_tex: Draw the base and the arm for the angle, then mark the second side along the arm.

If the angle is $180^\circ$ the arm points straight along the base, away from it, so the two sides lie on one line and joining the ends gives no triangle. Examples: $3\text{ cm}$, $180^\circ$, $7\text{ cm}$.

If the angle is more than $180^\circ$, for example $4\text{ cm}$, $210^\circ$, $6\text{ cm}$, the angle on the other side is less than $180^\circ$ and the picture is the same as a smaller angle; a measure of $180^\circ$ or more cannot be the angle of a triangle.
An angle of $0^\circ$ puts the arm on top of the base, so there is no triangle either.
For every angle strictly between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ the free ends can be joined, so a triangle always exists.

item.question: Say why no triangle can be built from the angles 90°, 5 cm, 90°, and from 100°, 5 cm, 95°.
steps: Draw the base of 5 cm.
With 90° at both ends the arms are straight up from the base, side by side. They never meet.
With 100° and 95° the arms lean outwards from the base, so they get further apart. They never meet.
Two angles that are each 90° or more always give arms that do not meet.
item.answer: No triangle: arms at 90° or more do not meet

item.question: The angle at A is 40°. Find the smallest angle at B for which the arms from A and B do not meet, and say whether the length AB matters.
steps_tex: Draw $AB$ and the arm from $A$ at $40^\circ$. Call the line along this arm $l$.
The arm from $B$ that does not meet $l$ and leans the least is the line $m$ parallel to $l$.
$AB$ is a transversal of the parallel lines $l$ and $m$. The angles on the same side add to $180^\circ$.
So $\angle B = 180^\circ - 40^\circ = 140^\circ$.
Any $\angle B$ of $140^\circ$ or more does not meet $l$; any $\angle B$ less than $140^\circ$ does. The length of $AB$ is not used anywhere.
item.answer_tex: $\angle B = 140^\circ$: no triangle when $\angle B$ is $140^\circ$ or more; the length of $AB$ does not matter

item.question: In triangle ABC, ∠B = 50° and ∠C = 70°. Using a line through A and parallel to BC, find ∠A.
steps_tex: Draw the line $XY$ through $A$, parallel to $BC$.
$\angle XAB$ and $\angle B$ are alternate angles, so $\angle XAB = 50^\circ$. $\angle YAC$ and $\angle C$ are alternate angles, so $\angle YAC = 70^\circ$.
$\angle XAB$, $\angle BAC$ and $\angle YAC$ together make the straight angle $XAY$: $50^\circ + \angle BAC + 70^\circ = 180^\circ$.
$120^\circ + \angle BAC = 180^\circ$, so $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$.
Construct to check: with $50^\circ$ at $B$ and $70^\circ$ at $C$, the angle measured at $A$ is $60^\circ$.
